title: Socket flush timing and proxy handoff labbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a labbook for a focused investigation into end-to-end latency added by socket flush timing and proxy handoff behavior in our inference path. We noticed unexplained 3–20ms tail bumps for short responses (<2kB) when traffic passes through the edge proxy + sidecar hop. Hypothesis is that client flush patterns, Nagle/TCP_NODELAY interactions, and HTTP/2 flow/window behaviors amplify small write stalls and cause micro-bursts at the proxy leading to queuing and extra scheduling overhead.

Scope / goals:
- Reproduce the short-response tail bump in a small, instrumented environment
- Isolate contributions from: application write size/timing, OS socket write coalescing, HTTP/2 frame packing and flow control, proxy buffer thresholds and flush pacing, and epoll/goroutine scheduling latency
- Measure distribution (p50/p90/p99) and characterize which combinations trigger multi-ms stalls
- Produce mitigations or config knobs to test in canary (e.g., explicit client flush, smaller write-chunks, proxy low/high watermark changes, keepalive tweaks)

Test harness and setup notes:
- Controlled cluster: 3 VM nodes (client, edge-proxy, backend-serving). Each VM: 8 vCPUs, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15 default tcp stack, tuned via sysctl when noted
- Edge proxy: custom NGINX-derived sidecar used in infra experiments branch + bench hooks (PR referenced above).
- Backend: Go-based inference stub that streams small chunks (text tokens) with configurable chunking and flush timing. Endpoint supports both HTTP/1.1 chunked responses and HTTP/2 streaming (grpc-web and native gRPC tested)
- Client: Go http2 and curl+nghttp2 for comparison, and a Python asyncio client to replicate real app behavior
- Workload: 10k requests, concurrency sweep (1, 4, 16, 64), payloads: tiny (200 bytes), small (1.2 kB), medium (12 kB). Short-circuit responses return within 2ms of request handling to focus on networking/streaming overhead

Key knobs exercised:
- TCP_NODELAY enabled/disabled on client and backend sockets
- Application-level flush frequency: immediate after each token, grouped every 50/200 tokens, or single flush for full response
- HTTP/2 SETTINGS_WINDOW_SIZE adjustments (default, +2x, -50%)
- Proxy buffer watermark: default, aggressive-flush (lower high-water mark), and batch-coalesce (higher threshold)
- Kernel write coalescing: tcp_slow_start_after_idle, net.ipv4.tcp_low_latency (on/off)

Profiling and instrumentation:
- Socket-level traces via bpftrace scripts that log write() syscall times and returned bytes, latency between successive write calls, and interval to kernel send completion
- Proxy internal timestamps (receive-first-byte, frame-queued, flush-to-backend) added to bench build
- Go pprof on backend to ensure context switches/goroutine stalls not dominating
- tcpdump on VM interfaces to observe TCP segments and packetization when needed

Representative results (raw observations):
- Baseline (no proxy, HTTP/2 native): tiny payloads, conc=16 -> p50=4.1ms, p90=6.8ms, p99=12.2ms
- With edge proxy (default config): tiny payloads, conc=16 -> p50=6.9ms, p90=11.0ms, p99=29.1ms (large p99 jump)
- Turning on TCP_NODELAY on both client and backend reduced p50 by ~0.9ms and p90 by ~1.7ms but p99 still elevated (~20–22ms)
- Application grouped flush every 50 tokens removed most p99 spikes; doing immediate flush per token produced highest p99
- Increasing HTTP/2 initial window to 2x reduced p99 by ~3–4ms in some runs; reducing window worsened p99 predictably
- Proxy aggressive-flush (low high-water) improved median slightly but increased CPU on proxy and made throughput lower at conc>=64 (backpressure oscillation)
- Observed packets: many small TCP segments when immediate flush used; long gaps (2–8ms) between application write() and kernel send completion in a subset of traces correlated with goroutine wake latency on proxy process (syscall-block->scheduler)

Interpretation / root cause sketch:
- Small writes + immediate flush interact badly with HTTP/2 frame packing and proxy buffering. The edge proxy tries to coalesce small frames to reduce overhead, but coalescing policy + flow control stalls can delay a frame until a threshold or timer fires, adding several ms.
- Nagle/TCP_NODELAY helps at the socket layer but does not eliminate the HTTP/2 framing/prioritization delays between proxy and backend.
- Proxy CPU contention and epoll wake scheduling accounted for a subset of largest p99s: when proxy thread was preempted or hit a syscall boundary, queued frames waited in user-space for the next wake.
- Backpressure feedback loops: under high concurrency, more client-side immediate flushes cause proxy to busy-wait less efficiently and trigger higher per-request latency variance. Aggressive proxy flushing reduces variance but increases CPU and packet rate (tradeoff).

Short actionable mitigations to validate in next sprint:
1) Client SDK: expose a sensible flush/coalescing policy default (group writes for <=5ms or 256 bytes, whichever comes first). This preserves low latency for single-shot flows but avoids pathological immediate-flush storms.
2) Proxy config: add an adaptive flush timer that shortens the coalesce timer when pending frames exceed X or when average inter-write interval is low. Tune high-water marks per machine class to avoid oscillatory backpressure.
3) Router/edge: mark short-response flows and route to a fast-path proxy instance with higher CPU allocation to reduce scheduling stalls.
4) Observability: add socket-level instrumentation to prod (sampled) so we can attribute p99 spikes to "flush pattern" vs "proxy scheduling" in customer traces

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How much of the problem is unique to our NGINX-derived proxy vs envoy/grpc-proxy? Need A/B test with envoy build
- Should we always enable TCP_NODELAY by default in SDKs? Side-effects on throughput need regression tests
- Are there interactions with TLS record coalescing and the TLS library that add another layer of buffering not yet measured? (next step: run with BoringTLS vs OpenSSL variants)

Notes for experiments to run next:
- Repeat with envoy and with a sparser CPU budget on proxy (1 core) to simulate stock infra; collect goroutine wake histograms
- Add a microbenchmark that toggles application write timing with jitter to mimic real model token emission patterns (burst vs uniform)
- Test python asyncio client patterns since prod clients often use non-Go runtimes

Appendix: quick commands used in harness (for reproducibility)
- run client: go run ./bench/client -concurrency=16 -payload=tiny -flush=immediate -url=https://edge-proxy.test/stream
- bpftrace snippet (write syscall timing): sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write /comm=="bench"/ { @[tid] = nsecs; } tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_write /comm=="bench"/ { printf("tid=%d elapsed=%d
", tid, nsecs-@[tid]); @[tid]=0 }'
- proxy logs: bench build with timestamps: make bench-proxy && ./proxy-bench --instrument > proxy.log

Conclusion / status:
Draft observations are consistent with a multi-layer buffering problem: immediate small writes propagate through socket, HTTP/2, and proxy buffers where coalescing and scheduling add ms-scale delays. Reasonable mitigations exist at SDK (coalesce), proxy (adaptive flush), and infra (fast-path for short flows). Next step: run envoy A/B, add TLS variation, and validate the SDK coalescing default in canary.

Author notes / TODO (personal):
- Clean up bpftrace scripts and add to repo under tools/networking/
- Push minimal SDK coalescing PR to candidates branch and run canary on dedicated cluster
- Document perf/observability signals to detect this class of issue in prod (add example query snippets)

End of labbook entry.
